extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and practitioners of media/journalism interested in news satire
extracted.subtask_description: A general encyclopedic overview of the genre of news satire: its definition, styles/types, history, modes of distribution, and practical issues (misidentification, editorial standards, controversy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation in mainstream journalism format
rubrics_metrics.description: News satire is 'a type of parody presented in a format typical of mainstream journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mimicking the look and conventions of legitimate news (headlines, bylines, inverted-pyramid structure, newsy tone) is a defining production choice that increases verisimilitude and comedic effect. The page notes this mimicry makes it 'relatively easy to mimic a legitimate news site' and underlies why satire can be mistaken for real news—creators should be aware of that tradeoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untrue content with satirical intent (distinct from fake news)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article frames news satire as 'untrue news with satirical intent' and contrasts it with 'Fake news' which has the intent to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative criterion is authorial intent: satire aims to parody/comment, whereas fake news aims to deceive. Producers and platforms should consider intent and labeling to differentiate satire from malicious misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: reliance on irony and deadpan humor
rubrics_metrics.description: News satire 'relies heavily on irony and deadpan humor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire often uses ironic contrast and a deadpan, straight-faced delivery to create humor. Tone is a primary stylistic criterion when judging the effectiveness of a piece; deadpan delivery increases believability and thus comedic impact but also raises risk of misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal types (approach): commentary/sketch vs wholly fictionalized stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Two slightly different types of news satire exist: one 'uses satirical commentary and sketch comedy to comment on real-world events,' and the other 'presents wholly fictionalized news stories.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating satire, identify which approach is used: commentary/satire of real events (more obviously topical) versus fictionalized news (which can be more prone to being taken as fact if styled closely to real reporting). Each approach has different ethical and editorial considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling/disclaimer requirement for print April Fools' satire
rubrics_metrics.description: When newspapers print news satire features (notably April Fools' Day pieces), 'This news is specifically identified somewhere in the paper or in the next day as a joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional print practice includes explicit identification to avoid deception; platforms and publishers should follow clear labeling/disclaimer practices when publishing satire to reduce confusion and potential harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of verisimilitude / accuracy of parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Some satires 'parodied news programs very accurately, so they were almost believable and could have been confused with actual news programs, if it was not for the fake stories reported.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-fidelity parody (accurate style, production values, and delivery) enhances comedic effect but also increases the risk that audiences or other media will mistake the content for real news. Evaluators should weigh comedic payoff against potential for misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of being picked up as real news and the importance of tagging
rubrics_metrics.description: The page documents multiple instances where satire was 'picked up as real by the media' and notes that 'Google News does mark such stories with a "satire" tag, not all readers notice the tag; moreover, sometimes satirical sources may not carry the tag.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical criterion for production/distribution is whether satire is clearly tagged and discoverable as satire across syndication channels. Failure to tag or to ensure tags propagate increases likelihood of misreporting by other outlets and social-network spread as factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/community admission standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hosted communities (example: HumorFeed) are 'notable for its relatively high standards of admission and active community involvement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality-control criteria for satire outlets can include editorial gatekeeping, community moderation, and admission standards for contributors. Strong standards reduce low-quality or misleading pieces and maintain a publication's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation and platform-account risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites satirical Twitter accounts being mistaken for legitimate sources (e.g., @Salondotcom parody) and notes incidents of impersonation reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should avoid impersonating real outlets/accounts in ways that may breach platform rules or laws. Platforms and creators must balance parody with clear signals that an account or post is satirical to avoid impersonation complaints and takedowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical focus and intended subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: News satire sites vary in focus—examples include celebrity/Hollywood entertainment (Hollywood Leek), political satire (The Onion, The Babylon Bee, regional examples), religious satire (Damascus Dropbear), and local/regional focuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of topical focus shapes tone, audience expectations, and risk profile: political satire may invite controversy or legal/political pressure (e.g., Bassem Youssef's program), while entertainment satire may be less politically fraught. Evaluators should consider alignment between subject matter and outlet identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential legal, political, and controversy risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire that 'pokes fun at powerful people' can be 'a source of tremendous controversy' and has led to investigations or blocking (examples: Bassem Youssef, Khabaristan Times blocked in Pakistan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and publishers must weigh freedom of expression and comedic aims against legal/political reprisals, censorship, and safety concerns. Risk assessment is a criterion when deciding topics, distribution jurisdictions, and attribution practices.
